Jean-Luc Godard. A Swiss-French filmmaker and theorist who became the most radical voice of the French New Wave, radically deconstructing narrative cinema through jump cuts, direct-to-camera address, and self-reflexive form. His early masterpiece Breathless broke every rule of conventional filmmaking and redefined what cinema could be, though his later work grew increasingly experimental and political.

He directed Breathless in 1960, the definitive French New Wave film that introduces abrupt jump cuts and an anti-hero protagonist played by Jean-Paul Belmondo. He pioneered the jump cut—sudden, unmotivated editing within scenes—as a signature technique that shattered continuity conventions. He wrote for Cahiers du cinéma, the influential film journal where New Wave directors nursed their auteur philosophy before making films.

Godard is known for fragmentary, essayistic narratives. His films often interrupt their own stories to digress into philosophy, literature, or formal experimentation. Later work grew increasingly political, embracing Marxist themes and renouncing conventional cinema as complicit in bourgeois ideology. He frequently cast Jean-Paul Belmondo and Anna Karina, his second wife, developing deep creative partnerships. He continued making films into the twenty-twenties, remaining one of cinema's most obstinate experimenters.

He shares with François Truffaut the role of fellow Cahiers critic and New Wave pioneer, the two representing opposite poles of the movement with Godard formal and Truffaut humanist. He was a contemporary experimenter with narrative form like Agnès Varda, and her work with documentary blending also influenced cinema. Jean-Pierre Melville was a precursor whose cool, economical style influenced Godard's approach. He helped define the nouvelle vague and then pushed beyond its own boundaries. Anna Karina was his actress and second wife, their collaborations defining much of his nineteen-sixties work.
